newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hyundai Motor profits seen hit by production cuts.
newsitem.headline: Hyundai Motor profits seen hit by production cuts.

text.p: Analysts sharply lowered profit forecasts for Hyundai Motor Co on Friday after South Korea's largest carmaker announced its first production cuts in 17 years.
Hyundai's car plant in the southern city of Ulsan is overflowing with unsold vehicles, and on Thursday the company said it would halt overtime work for five days to try to cut the stockpile.
The decision dramatically highlighted South Korea's economic woes. Domestic car sales have plummeted along with consumer confidence.
On Thursday finance minster Kang Kyong-shik acknowledged the economy was in "serious trouble".
Analysts said they believed other carmakers also would be forced to trim production for the first time since 1980, when the economy was reeling from the 1979 global oil shock.
Yang Dong-ki, an auto analyst at Donbang Peregrine Securities, said he was lowering his net profit forecast for Hyundai Motor in calendar 1997 to 149 billion won ($166.4 million) from 162 billion.
Kang Hoon-sok of ING Barings said he would drop his forecast to 200 billion won from 230 billion.
Hyundai's net almost halved to 86.8 billion won last year against 156.7 billion won after a 280 billion won extraordinary loss resulting from Canadian plant closures.
Its Ulsan plant normally runs two shifts of 10 hours each day. The shifts each include two hours of overtime, but these four extra hours will be cut for five days from April 8-12.
Hyundai said the cut would reduce inventories by 3,100 vehicles from about 67,000.
"Other carmakers will follow suit. I would not be surprised if they cut their production," said Kang at ING Barings.

"As the current level of inventories is too enormous to handle, domestic carmakers have no choice but to cut production," said Kim So-rim, the general manager of the Korea Automobile Manufacturers' Association.
Kim said the country's vehicle stockpile hit a record 180,000 units at the end of March from a previous record of 120,000 last October.
Production cuts at Hyundai Motor could not be sustained because of union objections, said Sohn Jong-won, motor analyst at Ssangyong Securiries.
Ironically, Hyundai Motor workers put in extra overtime following almost a month of sporadic nationwide strikes that began last December 26.
But their efforts to make up for lost production only resulted in a glut of unsold cars now jamming the piers and roads within South Korea's biggest car works.
Officials at Kia Motors and Daewoo Motor said they had no immediate plan to cut production.
"We can't imagine production cuts at the moment as we cannot fulfil soaring orders for new models," said Daewoo spokesman Lee Chang-won.
Analysts said South Korean carmakers would have to seek more export markets.

"The domestic market is saturated," said Jon Chong-hwa at Hanuri Salomon Securities. He forecast domestic vehicle demand would grow by only two to three percent this year from a 5.7 percent rise a year ago.
Industry figures show domestic auto sales fell 20.8 percent to 305,345 vehicles in the first quarter of this year.
(Conversion $1 = 895.40)
